Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Patricia was fifty-two when she finally walked into a therapist’s office, though she had been a judge for nearly a decade and had spent far longer learning to pass judgment on everything but herself. Fifteen years earlier, she had been a relief worker in a conflict zone—not a soldier, not a journalist, just someone who believed she could help. She had been part of a small medical convoy that was ambushed on a dusty road at dusk. The attackers wore uniforms, but not hers, and the first thing she tasted was the grit of sand and the metallic tang of blood from the driver beside her, whose body had slumped against her shoulder. She never learned what happened to the rest of the convoy; she only remembered the sound of gunfire, the shouting in a language she half-understood, and the absolute certainty that she was about to die. That certainty had not faded. When the memory came back, it came back whole—every sound, every smell, every terror—and she felt herself again in that moment, heart pounding, breath short, her mouth filled with that taste she could never scrub away.

For years after, Patricia told herself she had processed it. She had returned home, finished her law degree, built a career, married, divorced. She never spoke about the ambush. She learned to steer her thoughts away from it the way she steered her car away from dark streets after dusk—because being in the dark felt like being back on that road, waiting for the headlights to reveal what she could not face. She became a judge. The courtroom was supposed to be safe, a place of order and procedure. But every time a police officer or a military witness walked in, her stomach dropped. She would see the cut of the uniform, the way the fabric strained at the shoulder, and the memory would surge: the same shape, the same color, the same sickening recognition. She had come to believe that others could see it on her—that her fear was written across her face like a confession. During hearings, she would catch herself pressing her palms flat on the bench, trying to force her expression still, trying not to tremble. She controlled her emotions so tightly that her law clerk once asked if she ever felt anything at all.

The cost of that control was a growing distance. Colleagues invited her to dinner; she declined. Friends from her relief days reached out; she stopped returning calls. The world, she had decided, was a fundamentally dangerous place, and the only way to stay safe was to stay separate. She lived alone in a bright apartment with blinds drawn after sunset, and she ate carefully, avoiding foods that might bring back that taste. She never told anyone why she ordered the same bland meal every time she ate out. She never mentioned that the anniversary of the ambush came like a date carved into her bones, and that each year she would cancel her calendar, lock the door, and wait for the memories to hit.

What brought her to the clinic was a single morning in her chambers, three days after the fifteenth anniversary. She had been reviewing a motion when the sound of a helicopter passed overhead, and suddenly she was not in her courtroom—she was on that road, hearing the rotors of an approaching evacuation that never came. The terror was so total that she dropped her pen, and when her bailiff asked if she was all right, she could not speak. She had tried to suppress it, to tell herself it was just a memory, but her body would not listen. The isolation she had built to protect herself had begun to feel like a prison, and for the first time, she was more afraid of staying alone in it than she was of facing what she had survived. She came hoping that somewhere inside her there was a person who could taste food again without tasting dust, and who could walk into a courtroom and see a uniform without forgetting that not every stranger was a threat.
